lectureTitles: Why Did the Colonies Become Different?

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for England's move toward permanent colonization?

choices.text: Religious refugees created a single, unified demand for colonies.
choices.feedback: Religion mattered, but English colonization involved many actors who did not share one religious purpose.

choices.text: The Crown followed a complete imperial plan that had existed since the 1550s.
choices.feedback: England did not begin with a complete blueprint. Colonization developed through experiments, failures, and changing capacity.

choices.text: Religion, rivalry, profit, and migration opportunities converged as colonial capacity increased.
choices.feedback: This is the strongest explanation because it combines several motives with the growing ability to sustain settlements.

choices.text: The defeat of the Spanish Armada immediately gave England uncontested control of the Atlantic.
choices.feedback: The Armada mattered, but it did not destroy Spanish power or make permanent settlement automatic.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Permanent colonization grew from converging motives and increasing capacity, not one master cause.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for an explanation that combines motives with the ability to keep a settlement alive.
walkthrough: Identify the outcome: England moved from limited Atlantic ventures toward durable colonies.
Reject answers that reduce a long process to one group, one event, or one national plan.
Separate motives from capacity. Wanting a colony did not mean England could sustain one.
Choose the answer that explains why several motives became effective at the same time.
questions.transferStrategy: For a multi-cause question, choose the explanation that shows how causes interacted instead of selecting a favorite cause.
questions.hint: Ask which choice explains both why England wanted colonies and why permanent settlement became possible.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lecture 1 background essay and Reveal deck; Chapter 2 textbook, section 2-4
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: English colonization resulted from the convergence of religion, rivalry, profit, and opportunity, combined with greater colonial capacity.
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only synthesis of the lecture's central causal model.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image or specialist terminology is required.

questions.stem: Why did tobacco transform Virginia rather than simply make the colony profitable?

choices.text: It reduced the colony's need for workers and allowed settlements to remain compact.
choices.feedback: Tobacco increased labor demand and encouraged settlements to spread outward rather than remain compact.

choices.text: It linked profit to continuing demands for land and labor, expansion, inequality, and conflict.
choices.feedback: This is the strongest answer because it traces the wider chain of consequences created by the crop.

choices.text: It ended dependence on Atlantic markets by creating a self-sufficient local economy.
choices.feedback: Tobacco tied Virginia more closely to Atlantic markets. It did not create economic self-sufficiency.

choices.text: It made relations with Powhatan communities more stable by reducing competition for territory.
choices.feedback: Tobacco expansion increased pressure on Native land and made relations more dangerous.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Tobacco created a causal chain that reorganized land use, labor, settlement, and power.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Follow the consequences beyond the first increase in profit.
walkthrough: Start with the immediate result: tobacco became a profitable export.
Ask what profitable production required: fresh land and many workers.
Trace what those needs produced: expansion, bound labor, inequality, and conflict over territory.
Select the answer that explains the whole chain, not only the first step.
questions.transferStrategy: For a consequence question, trace the chain beyond the immediate effect and identify what changed in society and power.
questions.hint: Use the lecture chain: Tobacco to Profit to Land to Labor to Expansion.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lecture 2 background essay, Reveal deck, and Historian's Notebook; Chapter 2 textbook, section 2-5
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Tobacco reorganized Virginia around land-intensive export production, bound labor, expansion, and conflict over Native land.
sourceAlignment.notes: Tests consequence rather than recall of John Rolfe or a date.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. The causal chain is stated in ordinary language.

questions.stem: Which comparison best explains why Virginia and New England became different societies?

choices.text: Virginia preserved English society, while New England rejected all English institutions.
choices.feedback: Both regions adapted English institutions. Neither simply preserved or rejected England as a whole.

choices.text: Virginia was shaped only by profit, while New England was shaped only by religion.
choices.feedback: Motives mattered, but this comparison ignores environment, migration, labor, and economic connections.

choices.text: Virginia had no families, while New England had no commercial ambitions.
choices.feedback: Both statements are too absolute. The regions differed in proportions and patterns, not through complete absence.

choices.text: Different goals, environments, migration streams, and labor systems interacted in each region.
choices.feedback: This is the strongest comparison because it uses the same four variables for both regions and explains their interaction.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The regions diverged because the same four variables combined differently in each place.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Use the same basis of comparison for both regions and avoid single-cause contrasts.
walkthrough: Identify the two cases: Virginia and New England.
Use the same categories for both cases rather than changing the basis of comparison.
Avoid absolute claims such as 'only,' 'all,' or 'none.'
Choose the answer that explains how goals, environment, migration, and labor reinforced one another.
questions.transferStrategy: For comparison, apply the same categories to both cases and explain how the differences produced different outcomes.
questions.hint: Recall the lecture formula: Goals + Environment + Migration + Labor = Colonial Society.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lecture 2 background essay, Reveal deck, and Historian's Notebook; Chapter 2 textbook, sections 2-5 and 2-6
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Colonial societies developed through the interaction of goals, environment, migration, and labor.
sourceAlignment.notes: Directly rehearses the lecture's comparative model without copying an exam item.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only comparison with parallel answer choices.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes religious freedom and religious toleration in Massachusetts Bay?

choices.text: Puritans wanted freedom to build a godly community but limited competing religious practices.
choices.feedback: This is the strongest answer because it distinguishes freedom for a community from toleration of disagreement within it.

choices.text: Puritans rejected any connection between religious belief and civil government.
choices.feedback: Puritan institutions linked religious purpose to family, town, education, and government.

choices.text: Massachusetts Bay welcomed religious pluralism but restricted Puritan worship.
choices.feedback: This reverses the historical pattern. Puritans could practice their faith, while dissenters faced serious limits.

choices.text: Religious freedom and religious toleration meant the same thing to seventeenth-century Puritans.
choices.feedback: The lecture treats these as different ideas. Confusing them hides the logic of the Puritan commonwealth.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Massachusetts protected a Puritan community's religious project without embracing modern pluralism.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Hold freedom for a religious community apart from toleration of competing beliefs.
walkthrough: Define religious freedom in the Puritan setting: freedom to establish and practice a godly community.
Define toleration: allowing people with competing beliefs to practice within the same political community.
Compare the definitions with Massachusetts policy toward dissent.
Choose the answer that preserves both the Puritans' real freedom and the limits they placed on others.
questions.transferStrategy: For context, use the meanings historical actors gave to ideas rather than automatically importing modern definitions.
questions.hint: Which choice separates 'our community may practice' from 'people who disagree may also practice'?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lecture 3 background essay, Reveal deck, and Historian's Notebook; Chapter 2 textbook, section 2-6
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Puritan New England expanded religious freedom for Puritans while restricting broader religious toleration.
sourceAlignment.notes: Uses the central distinction students practiced in class.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. Key terms are defined in the walkthrough.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the claim that colonial government was representative but not modern democracy?

choices.text: Colonies had elected bodies, and every adult resident could vote and hold office.
choices.feedback: The first part is true, but the second is not. Political participation remained limited by status, sex, religion, race, and property.

choices.text: Colonial assemblies existed only in name and never influenced taxation or local law.
choices.feedback: Assemblies exercised real power and helped create expectations of local participation.

choices.text: Assemblies and town meetings gave some colonists a voice while excluding much of the population.
choices.feedback: This directly supports both parts of the claim: meaningful representation and restricted political equality.

choices.text: The Crown allowed colonies to become independent republics during the seventeenth century.
choices.feedback: Colonies remained within a monarchical and imperial order. Local participation did not equal independence.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The evidence shows real participation inside a political community with firm boundaries.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. The best evidence must support both representation and exclusion at the same time.
walkthrough: Break the claim into two parts: representative government and limited democracy.
Reject evidence that supports only one part or makes an absolute claim.
Look for evidence of elected institutions together with restricted membership.
Choose the answer that directly supports the entire claim.
questions.transferStrategy: For evidence, select the choice that directly supports every important part of the claim, not merely the topic in general.
questions.hint: The strongest evidence must show both participation and exclusion.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lecture 4 background essay, Reveal deck, and Historian's Notebook; Chapter 2 textbook discussion of colonial governments
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Assemblies and town governments built habits of local participation without establishing broad political equality.
sourceAlignment.notes: Evidence question based on the lecture's caution against calling early institutions modern democracy.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item with one claim divided into two explicit parts.

questions.stem: An English promoter wants a permanent colony rather than a seasonal raiding base. Which plan best applies the lesson of Roanoke?

choices.text: Provide reliable resupply, varied skills, families, and workable Native relations.
choices.feedback: This plan addresses the connected capacities that a permanent settlement required.

choices.text: Send a small military force and assume nearby communities will provide food indefinitely.
choices.feedback: Roanoke showed that military purpose and expectations of Native support could not substitute for sustainable planning.

choices.text: Rely on a royal charter because legal possession guarantees local survival.
choices.feedback: A charter could authorize a venture, but it could not supply food, labor, diplomacy, or reliable shipping.

choices.text: Wait for one decisive victory over Spain before attempting any settlement.
choices.feedback: English colonial ventures began before the Armada, and military victory did not automatically create settlement capacity.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The lesson of Roanoke is that permanent settlement required a connected system of support.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Apply the distinction between claiming territory and sustaining a community.
walkthrough: Identify the model being applied: Roanoke failed through interdependent weaknesses.
List what a settlement needs that a raid does not: food, people, skills, resupply, financing, and diplomacy.
Reject plans that treat legal authority or military purpose as sufficient.
Choose the plan that strengthens several capacities at once.
questions.transferStrategy: When applying a historical model, identify the mechanism that produced the earlier outcome and look for the choice that changes that mechanism.
questions.hint: A permanent colony had to solve several problems at the same time, not merely receive permission to exist.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lecture 1 background essay, Reveal deck, and Historian's Notebook; Chapter 2 textbook, section 2-4
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Roanoke exposed the logistical, diplomatic, environmental, financial, and demographic requirements of permanent settlement.
sourceAlignment.notes: Bounded application scenario; no free-floating counterfactual claim.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only scenario. The scenario is short and contains one decision.

questions.stem: A colony discovers a labor-intensive export crop that quickly exhausts nearby soil. Based on Virginia's pattern, what is most likely to happen next?

choices.text: The colony will reduce production so that land and labor become less important.
choices.feedback: A profitable export usually gives producers incentives to expand production rather than voluntarily reduce it.

choices.text: The colony will shift immediately to family farms and end its dependence on Atlantic trade.
choices.feedback: The scenario points toward deeper export dependence and labor demand, not an immediate shift away from them.

choices.text: The colony will become politically equal because profitable crops distribute wealth evenly.
choices.feedback: Plantation exports often concentrated land, labor control, and political influence rather than distributing them evenly.

choices.text: Demand for fresh land and workers will grow, pushing settlement outward and increasing conflict.
choices.feedback: This applies the Virginia model: export profit creates continuing land and labor pressures with political consequences.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The crop's ecology and labor demands would likely reproduce Virginia's expansionary chain.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Predict what profitable production requires, then follow those requirements outward.
walkthrough: Identify the relevant model: profitable staple crop plus soil exhaustion plus labor intensity.
Infer the direct needs: more acreage and more workers.
Infer the broader effects: outward settlement, labor coercion, inequality, and conflict over land.
Choose the answer that follows the model without adding an unsupported result.
questions.transferStrategy: For prediction, carry forward the causal mechanism that was taught rather than guessing from surface similarities.
questions.hint: What happens when profit depends on both fresh soil and a large workforce?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lecture 2 background essay, Reveal deck, and Historian's Notebook; Chapter 2 textbook, section 2-5
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: The tobacco model links export profit to land, labor, expansion, and conflict.
sourceAlignment.notes: New bounded scenario applies the taught causal chain without duplicating Virginia wording exactly.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only scenario with no numerical calculation.

questions.stem: Massachusetts leaders believe public religious dissent threatens their covenant with God. Which response best fits their political logic?

choices.text: Treat every religious claim as a private matter beyond any concern of the community.
choices.feedback: Puritan society did not sharply separate private religion from public order in this way.

choices.text: Restrict dissent to protect the colony's shared religious order.
choices.feedback: This response follows the logic of a godly commonwealth built around shared truth and collective obligation.

choices.text: End town government because participation is incompatible with religious authority.
choices.feedback: Puritan New England combined bounded participation with strong religious assumptions; it did not abandon local government.

choices.text: Ask the English bishops to impose uniform worship on Massachusetts from overseas.
choices.feedback: Puritans migrated partly to escape episcopal control and build their own reformed institutions.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Within Puritan assumptions, dissent could appear as a public threat to a covenanted community.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Apply the Puritans' own connection between religious truth, covenant, and public order.
walkthrough: Identify the actors' assumptions rather than starting with modern church-state separation.
Recall that covenant linked religious purpose to community institutions.
Ask how leaders would interpret dissent inside a society organized around shared truth.
Choose the response that fits their historical logic without claiming it was modern liberal policy.
questions.transferStrategy: For actor perspective, reconstruct the choices available within the actor's own assumptions before judging the decision.
questions.hint: In a covenanted society, leaders could treat religious disagreement as a problem for the whole community.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lecture 3 background essay, Reveal deck, and Historian's Notebook; Chapter 2 textbook, section 2-6
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: A community built around shared religious truth found dissent difficult to tolerate.
sourceAlignment.notes: Applies the lecture model without asking students to endorse the policy.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only actor-perspective item. The historical assumptions are stated in the stem.

questions.stem: A Native sachem understands an agreement as an alliance with shared land use. English settlers treat it as permanent submission and exclusive ownership. Which concept best explains the dispute?

choices.text: A disagreement caused only by poor translation of individual words.
choices.feedback: Language could matter, but the deeper conflict involved different political and legal meanings of land and authority.

choices.text: A simple conflict between people who understood property and people who did not.
choices.feedback: Native communities had their own systems of territory, use rights, diplomacy, and political authority.

choices.text: Overlapping sovereignty and different understandings of what the agreement authorized.
choices.feedback: This captures the conflict between competing claims to govern, use land, and define political relationships.

choices.text: Proof that the Crown already exercised complete control over every colonial land transaction.
choices.feedback: Imperial authority was incomplete, and local agreements were often negotiated among several political actors.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The same agreement could carry different meanings within overlapping political worlds.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look beyond vocabulary to competing claims about land, alliance, and political authority.
walkthrough: Identify what each side believes the agreement changes.
Notice that the disagreement concerns authority and land, not merely one translated phrase.
Reject the idea that only one side possessed political or property concepts.
Choose the concept that allows several legitimate claims to overlap and collide.
questions.transferStrategy: For context, identify the political systems and legal meanings surrounding an agreement before treating its words as self-explanatory.
questions.hint: The lecture describes early America as a field of competing jurisdictions rather than one settled hierarchy.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lecture 4 background essay, Reveal deck, and Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Land transactions could be understood differently within overlapping Native and English systems of sovereignty and jurisdiction.
sourceAlignment.notes: New scenario applies the lecture's sovereignty framework.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only scenario. 'Sovereignty' is explained through feedback and walkthrough.

questions.stem: A proprietor governs a colony without an elected assembly, but many settlers are accustomed to local representation. What response is most likely?

choices.text: Settlers will press for an assembly and resist taxation that lacks local representative approval.
choices.feedback: This applies the pattern seen in colonies where local practice became an expected political right.

choices.text: Settlers will reject all English legal traditions and demand immediate national independence.
choices.feedback: Colonists usually defended English rights and local institutions long before seeking independence.

choices.text: Settlers will accept the arrangement because a proprietor's charter removes all need for consent.
choices.feedback: Chartered authority did not prevent settlers from bargaining, petitioning, and resisting policies they considered illegitimate.

choices.text: Settlers will transfer authority to neighboring Native nations rather than seek colonial institutions.
choices.feedback: Native nations remained political actors, but settler demands for representation focused on colonial assemblies and taxation.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Repeated local participation turned representation from a concession into an expectation.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Apply the pattern of negotiated authority between top-down claims and established local practice.
walkthrough: Identify the conflict: delegated proprietary power versus settler expectations of representation.
Recall that colonists often defended local taxation and lawmaking through assemblies.
Reject answers that jump prematurely to independence or erase colonial political traditions.
Choose the likely response produced by established habits of local government.
questions.transferStrategy: When applying an institutional pattern, ask what repeated practice has taught people to regard as legitimate authority.
questions.hint: What happens when settlers begin treating an old concession as a political right?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lecture 4 background essay and Reveal deck; Chapter 2 textbook, section 2-7
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Settler expectations of representation repeatedly collided with proprietary and royal efforts at top-down control.
sourceAlignment.notes: Uses a generalized scenario derived from New York and the lecture's negotiated-authority model.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only institutional application item.

questions.stem: Which connection best explains why Jamestown survived crises that would probably have ended an earlier venture such as Roanoke?

choices.text: Jamestown faced no major problems with food, disease, leadership, or Native relations.
choices.feedback: Jamestown suffered severe mortality, hunger, warfare, and institutional failures.

choices.text: Repeatedly resupply the colony, absorb losses, and revise institutions.
choices.feedback: This connects Lecture 1's growing colonial capacity with Lecture 2's account of Jamestown as institutional learning.

choices.text: Jamestown succeeded because its original 1607 plan accurately predicted the Chesapeake environment.
choices.feedback: The colony survived by revising assumptions and institutions, not by executing a flawless original design.

choices.text: The Powhatan political world immediately accepted permanent English sovereignty over the region.
choices.feedback: Early relations involved dependence, diplomacy, incompatible claims, and eventually war.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Jamestown's survival linked greater English capacity to repeated institutional adaptation.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Connect the difference between colonial ambition and the ability to survive repeated failure.
walkthrough: Recall Lecture 1's distinction between wanting a colony and sustaining one.
Recall Lecture 2's description of Jamestown as a near catastrophe and a process of adaptation.
Look for an answer that uses evidence from both lectures.
Choose the connection that explains survival without pretending Jamestown was well designed from the start.
questions.transferStrategy: For a Connect question, identify one idea from each lecture and explain the causal bridge between them.
questions.hint: Roanoke shows limited capacity; Jamestown shows what repeated resupply and institutional revision made possible.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lectures 1 and 2 background essays and Reveal decks; Chapter 2 textbook, sections 2-4 and 2-5
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: By the seventeenth century, greater migration, capital, shipping, and institutional adaptation allowed colonies to survive disasters that had ended earlier ventures.
sourceAlignment.notes: Genuine cross-lecture causal synthesis.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only cross-lecture item.

questions.stem: How does the Great Migration help connect the regional model from Lecture 2 to the Puritan society examined in Lecture 3?

choices.text: It brought mainly isolated young laborers, which made New England resemble early Virginia.
choices.feedback: New England received proportionately more families and social institutions than early Virginia.

choices.text: It removed New England from Atlantic trade and made the region economically self-sufficient.
choices.feedback: New England remained connected to Atlantic commerce, including trade with plantation colonies.

choices.text: It brought families, skills, capital, and leaders who could sustain towns, churches, schools, and households.
choices.feedback: This connects migration patterns to the institutions and demographic stability of Puritan New England.

choices.text: It made all residents full church members and eliminated disagreement within Puritan communities.
choices.feedback: Church membership remained selective, and dissent and generational change continued.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Migration supplied the human infrastructure that made the Puritan institutional project durable.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Connect who migrated with the kind of community those migrants could build.
walkthrough: Start with Lecture 2's migration variable in the regional model.
Identify the distinctive New England migration pattern: more families and varied skills.
Connect that population to Lecture 3's institutions: households, towns, churches, and schools.
Choose the answer that explains how migration supported the society, not merely who arrived.
questions.transferStrategy: For comparison across lectures, connect a structural variable in one lecture to the institutions or outcomes explained in another.
questions.hint: Ask what kinds of institutions become easier to build when whole households and community leaders migrate together.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lectures 2 and 3 background essays, Reveal decks, and Historian's Notebook; Chapter 2 textbook, section 2-6
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Family migration and healthier demographic conditions helped New England become a self-reproducing society organized through towns, households, and congregations.
sourceAlignment.notes: Genuine synthesis of migration and institution building.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only comparison.

questions.stem: Which development best connects Virginia's tobacco economy to the chapter's larger problem of sovereignty?

choices.text: Tobacco kept English settlement compact, allowing Native and English territorial claims to remain separate.
choices.feedback: Tobacco encouraged dispersed plantations and continuing expansion into Native territory.

choices.text: Tobacco made land less politically important because wealth came only from overseas trade.
choices.feedback: Export profit depended on control of local land and labor, making territory more politically important.

choices.text: Tobacco ended colonial interest in representative institutions by concentrating attention on farming.
choices.feedback: Virginia developed representative institutions while plantation expansion continued.

choices.text: Tobacco drove expansion into Native homelands, strengthening settler power while narrowing Native political autonomy.
choices.feedback: This links the economic chain of Lecture 2 to the competing sovereignty claims of Lecture 4.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Economic expansion changed the balance of political authority over land.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Connect the crop's demand for territory with who could govern and control that territory.
walkthrough: Recall what tobacco required: land, workers, and outward settlement.
Recall what sovereignty concerns: governing people, territory, diplomacy, and political independence.
Ask how expansion changed the ability of Native nations and settlers to exercise authority.
Choose the answer that links economic growth to a shift in political power.
questions.transferStrategy: For consequence across topics, ask how an economic process changes who controls land, labor, institutions, or decision making.
questions.hint: The lecture's key tension is that settler self-government expanded as Indigenous sovereignty contracted.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lectures 2 and 4 background essays, Reveal decks, and Historian's Notebook; Chapter 2 textbook, section 2-5
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Tobacco expansion increased pressure on Native territory and helped shift authority toward settler governments.
sourceAlignment.notes: Cross-lecture consequence linking political economy and sovereignty.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only synthesis. 'Sovereignty' is contextualized in the walkthrough.

questions.stem: Which pattern appears in both Puritan institutions and early colonial representative government?

choices.text: Participation operated inside communities that set firm boundaries on membership and authority.
choices.feedback: This connects congregational and town participation with representative institutions that excluded much of the population.

choices.text: Political and religious participation was open equally to every adult living in the colonies.
choices.feedback: Both religious and political membership were bounded by status, belief, sex, race, and other qualifications.

choices.text: Local participation eliminated hierarchy in churches, households, towns, and colonial governments.
choices.feedback: Participation coexisted with strong hierarchies and unequal authority.

choices.text: Consent mattered only in civil government and had no role in Puritan congregations or towns.
choices.feedback: Puritan churches and towns also used forms of election, covenant, written rules, and local participation.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Participation was real, but it functioned within bounded and unequal communities.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for the pattern that preserves both participation and exclusion.
walkthrough: Identify Lecture 3's participatory institutions: congregations, covenants, and town government.
Identify Lecture 4's representative institutions: assemblies, elections, and local taxation.
Compare what both allowed and whom both excluded.
Choose the pattern that avoids calling either system fully democratic or wholly authoritarian.
questions.transferStrategy: For comparison, preserve tension when the evidence shows two features operating at the same time.
questions.hint: Both lectures resist the false choice between participation and hierarchy.

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 2 Lectures 3 and 4 background essays, Reveal decks, and Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Puritan and colonial institutions combined consent and local participation with bounded membership and unequal authority.
sourceAlignment.notes: Cross-lecture comparison based on the course's nuance about democracy and theocracy.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only comparison with parallel choices.

questions.stem: Which chapter-level claim best connects all four lectures?

choices.text: English colonization followed one shared plan and produced the same society wherever settlers arrived.
choices.feedback: The lectures emphasize converging motives, experimentation, regional difference, and competing authorities.

choices.text: Colonization expanded settler opportunity and participation while producing coercion, exclusion, and land conflict.
choices.feedback: This claim connects motive, regional development, Puritan institutions, labor systems, and contested sovereignty.

choices.text: Religious ideas alone determined colonial economies, migration patterns, labor systems, and political authority.
choices.feedback: Religion mattered greatly, but the chapter repeatedly uses multi-cause explanations involving environment, markets, migration, labor, and power.

choices.text: By 1680 the Crown had created a centralized empire that fully controlled colonists and Native nations.
choices.feedback: Authority remained layered and negotiated among the Crown, proprietors, colonists, and Native nations.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Chapter 2 shows expansion creating liberty and capacity for some through systems that constrained others.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. The best synthesis must preserve the chapter's multiple causes, regional differences, and unequal power.
walkthrough: Recall Lecture 1: different motives converged, and opportunity was distributed unequally.
Recall Lecture 2: profit and labor systems produced both opportunity and coercion.
Recall Lecture 3: a participatory religious community limited dissent and expanded into Native homelands.
Recall Lecture 4: settler representation grew amid contested sovereignty and imperial claims.
Choose the claim broad enough to connect all four without erasing their differences.
questions.transferStrategy: For chapter synthesis, build a claim that explains several lectures while preserving important tensions and exceptions.
questions.hint: Which choice can include both expanding settler institutions and the unequal costs of colonial expansion?

questions.stem: Why did the defeat of the Spanish Armada matter without by itself causing English colonization?

choices.text: It weakened a major rival and increased confidence, but colonies still required money, migrants, shipping, and organization.
choices.feedback: This treats the Armada as one enabling condition inside a larger causal chain.

choices.text: It immediately created Jamestown in 1588, as an explanation of the broader historical pattern.
choices.feedback: Jamestown began in 1607, and a naval victory did not create a settlement by itself.

choices.text: It ended religious conflict inside England, as an explanation of the broader historical pattern.
choices.feedback: Religious conflict continued and helped shape migration and imperial rivalry.

choices.text: It proved that raiding Spanish ships and building colonies required the same capacity, as an explanation of the broader historical pattern.
choices.feedback: Raiding could succeed without the supply systems and institutions needed for settlement.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. This is the strongest cause answer.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Focus on the cause relationship the question is testing.

Separate the strongest explanation from a trigger, consequence, or related detail.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the claim that Roanoke exposed a problem of colonial capacity?

choices.text: Some English people wanted religious reform, as an explanation of the broader historical pattern.
choices.feedback: Religious motives were important, but they do not directly demonstrate Roanoke's supply problem.

choices.text: The settlement lacked reliable resupply, stable financing, enough people, and secure diplomatic relationships.
choices.feedback: Those linked shortages directly explain why a lasting colony was difficult to sustain.

choices.text: English sailors had already raided Spanish shipping, as an explanation of the broader historical pattern.
choices.feedback: Successful raiding shows naval reach, not the full capacity to maintain a colony.

choices.text: Roanoke was located in North America, as an explanation of the broader historical pattern.
choices.feedback: Location alone does not explain the venture's logistical failure.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. This is the strongest evidence answer.
